metaDescription: Five snow blowers under $1000 compared: two-stage gas from Husqvarna and PowerSmart, two EGO cordless kits and a brushless corded unit.
expertTake: The Husqvarna ST124 is the pick for deep, heavy snow because it pairs a 212cc engine with a 21-inch intake and a ribbon auger that handles packed snow. The EGO 21-inch Peak Power cordless is the best battery machine if you want gas-like throw without fuel. Skip this budget if your driveway is short and level, since a cheaper corded machine will do the job.
introParagraphs: At this ceiling the question is not whether you can afford a snow blower but which kind fits your winters. Two-stage gas machines remain the answer for deep or heavy snow, while premium cordless units answer the question of quiet, fuel-free convenience.

Mixing the two categories in one list shows how different the tradeoffs are. Prices move and the $1000 cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated, so check the live number before you commit.

products.name: Husqvarna ST124 24-Inch 212cc Two-Stage Snow Blower
products.description:
The ST124 is a conventional two-stage gas machine built around a 212cc engine and a 24-inch housing. A ribbon auger mixes air into the snow, which makes it easier to handle than a solid auger, and the 21-inch intake height lets it swallow drifts that would stop a single-stage unit cold. The 13-inch snow tires give grip and control on a slope.

The tradeoff is weight, noise and upkeep. Compared with the EGO cordless options in this guide, it starts with a pull cord or primer rather than a button, needs fuel and oil, and is far heavier to store. In return it throws snow with an impeller rather than relying on an auger scraping the pavement, so it works on gravel with skid shoes set high and does not care about battery size.

Every autumn, change the oil, replace the spark plug and use fresh fuel with stabilizer. Carry spare shear pins, because a frozen chunk of ice in the auger will break one before it breaks the gearbox. Storage is the part buyers underestimate: a two-stage of this size needs a corner of the garage roughly the footprint of a small lawn mower, and it is heavy enough that loading it into a truck takes a ramp. If you live where snow arrives in October and lingers into April, that is a fair price for a machine that rarely stalls. Skid shoes are worth adjusting to the surface each season, because set too low they dig into gravel and too high they leave a skin of ice.
products.bestFor: Deep, heavy or plowed-in snow on long driveways.
cons: Requires fuel, oil and plug service

products.name: EGO Power+ 21-Inch Single-Stage Cordless, Two 6Ah
products.description:
This EGO combines two 56V ARC batteries in Peak Power mode to drive a 21-inch steel auger. The listing states a throw of up to 45 feet and a capacity to clear a 14-car driveway of 8 inches, which are best-case claims but show how much energy two 6Ah packs hold. Steel augers stand up to ice chunks better than plastic.

Compared with the SNT2122, it carries larger 6Ah packs rather than 4Ah, so it should run longer before you swap. Against the Husqvarna it gives up the ability to handle deep snow, but it starts at the push of a button and needs no fuel or oil.

Store the packs indoors, keep the charger vents clear and take heavy snow in layers. It is the machine to buy if you value quiet, quick starts and a clean garage. If you own other EGO tools the packs cross over, which brings the real cost of ownership down. Expect to retire the packs after several winters of hard use, and budget for replacement at that point rather than assuming the first set lasts forever. Another point in its favor is balance: the 6Ah packs let you take a normal storm in one outing, which is how most people measure a good cordless day. Keep the electric start cord dry and test it in autumn, since a frayed cord is a poor discovery at six in the morning.
products.bestFor: Premium cordless buyers with moderate snowfall and paved drives.
cons: High cost compared with corded options

products.name: PowerSmart 24-Inch 212cc Two-Stage Gas Snow Blower
products.description:
The PowerSmart is a 24-inch two-stage machine with a 212cc snow engine and a push-button start fed from a 120V outlet. The maker claims 2400 pounds per minute, a ceiling that is far above any electric single-stage in this guide, and a self-propelled drive saves you from pushing.

Against the Husqvarna, it lists a similar engine and width but a lesser-known brand, so check parts and warranty terms. Against the EGO cordless, it offers deep-snow ability and unlimited runtime for the same cap.

The electric start needs an extension cord to the garage, so keep a pull cord working too. Do the usual gas chores: fresh fuel, oil, plug and shear pins. A practical test before buying is to ask whether you can get a pull cord replacement and drive belts through a local shop. For a lesser-known brand that answer decides whether a simple repair takes a day or a month, so read the warranty and photograph the serial plate on arrival. Compared with the Husqvarna, it is the better value if you want push-button start and accept a less known name, but verify the claimed throughput against your own snow. Wipe the discharge chute with a silicone spray before storms so wet snow slides out instead of sticking.
products.bestFor: Heavy snow on a budget with an engine you are willing to maintain.
cons: Brand is less established than Husqvarna

products.name: STEELITE 20-Inch Corded Brushless Snow Blower 15A
products.description:
The STEELITE corded unit uses a 15 amp brushless motor, a 20-inch path and a 10-inch intake. The listing notes that it needs a power cord, which is not included, so factor in a suitable extension. Brushless design cuts wear and keeps power steady under load.

It is the least expensive and simplest machine in this list. Compared with the cordless EGO machines it has no battery to manage, and compared with the gas two-stage units it is far lighter.

Its limit is reach and depth: a cord is a nuisance on a long driveway, and a single-stage cannot handle plow ridges. If you buy it, measure your longest extension cord and confirm it is rated for 15 amps outdoors. A thin cord will overheat and cut power, and no brushless motor can fix that. Store the machine dry and wipe the housing before parking it for the season. Because it is a corded unit with no battery, it will sit untouched all summer and start without any coaxing the following winter. Never use a corded machine in standing water, and plug it into a GFCI outlet.
products.bestFor: Short paved drives near an outlet.

products.name: EGO Power+ SNT2122 21-Inch Cordless Kit
products.description:
The SNT2122 is a complete cordless kit with two 4Ah packs and a 320W charger. Variable auger speed and a 180-degree chute give control, and the maker claims it clears a ten-car driveway of 8 inches.

It costs less than the 6Ah EGO but offers less runtime. If your driveway is short, the smaller packs are plenty and the machine saves money.

Keep the packs inside and the vents clear. Its smaller packs are the compromise: they are plenty for a short drive and a walk, but a double-wide driveway after a heavy storm may need a pause and a swap. Buy a third pack only if your runs regularly exceed what two give you, since extra packs cost far more than the machine's price difference suggests. If you want to step up later, the same charger and packs work with other EGO tools. Wipe the battery contacts occasionally with a dry cloth to maintain a clean connection.
products.bestFor: Moderate driveways where a smaller kit is enough.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Husqvarna ST124 and PowerSmart are two-stage: an auger feeds an impeller. They handle snow deeper than 12 inches and plow ridges. The EGO machines and the STEELITE are single-stage and suit up to roughly 8 inches. If you see regular deep storms, buy two-stage. Check your largest plow ridge: if it is taller than about 10 inches, a single-stage will not cope with it however many batteries it has.

The ST124 lists a 21-inch intake, which lets it take drifts in one pass. The STEELITE lists 10 inches, a typical single-stage figure. Intake height times width tells you how much snow one pass can handle.

The PowerSmart has a 120V electric start, which helps in cold weather but requires an outlet and a cord. Pull-start machines are simpler but harder in subzero cold. Cordless models start with a button. In subzero cold, a gas engine also wants a few primer pushes and a full warm-up, so budget a few extra minutes.

The EGO 21-inch includes two 6Ah packs while the SNT2122 includes two 4Ah. The larger packs hold 50 percent more charge, which is the difference between finishing a long driveway and stopping to charge. Add up how many passes your driveway needs and compare that with the quoted charge capacity.

Husqvarna and EGO are established brands with dealers and parts networks. PowerSmart and STEELITE are less known. In year three that matters when you need a belt, scraper or battery. Ask a local dealer if they stock belts and shear pins for the model before you buy.

Two-stage machines use wheels or tracks. The ST124 has 13-inch snow tires. On a slope, traction matters more than engine size. Walk your steepest slope in boots first; if you slip, a machine with 13-inch tires will help far more than a bigger engine.

specDecoder.meaning: Larger displacement gives more torque, but design matters too. 212cc is typical for a 24-inch two-stage.
specDecoder.watchFor: The ST124 and PowerSmart both list 212cc.

specDecoder.meaning: A throughput ceiling under ideal conditions.
A boost that draws from both packs when the motor is under load.
An open-spiral auger that mixes air into snow, making it easier to move.
A motor without carbon brushes. It has less wear and steadier power.
specDecoder.watchFor: The STEELITE corded unit lists a brushless motor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Snow capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared intake height and machine type. The ST124's 21-inch intake sets the top end. Single-stage units were compared on width. Intake height turned out to be the best single predictor of deep-snow ability.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated gas, cordless and corded options. Each has different upkeep. Kits with larger packs were favored. We checked whether each listing includes everything needed to start working on day one.

howWeEvaluated.title: Brand maturity
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the maker's parts network. Husqvarna and EGO lead. Others carry a risk of thinner support. Dealer and parts access were weighted heavily for the gas machines.

howWeEvaluated.title: Starting and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at electric start, drive systems and tires. Self-propelled machines ease the work. Cordless units are easier to handle. Starting method matters in subzero mornings, so we compared push-button and pull-start designs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value within the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at features per price band. Two-stage gas gives the most capability, premium cordless the most convenience. A well-priced gas two-stage can beat a premium cordless on total capability, which we kept in view.

cards.label: Gas
cards.text: The Husqvarna ST124 and PowerSmart offer unlimited runtime and deep-snow power. They need fuel, oil and plug service, and they are heavy.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: The two EGO machines start instantly and are quiet. Runtime depends on pack size, and they are limited to moderate snow.

howToChoose.note: Choose gas for heavy winters; choose cordless for convenience.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A 24-inch path, self-propelled drive and either gas or large battery capacity.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Husqvarna ST124 and PowerSmart both fit. The EGO 21-Inch with 6Ah packs is the best cordless choice for long runs.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You face deep snow or want a trusted dealer network. The Husqvarna is the premium pick.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your snow is light. The STEELITE corded or EGO SNT2122 is enough.

maintenance.why: Cold starts thin oil. Fresh oil protects the engine.
A fouled plug causes hard starts.
Spare pins save a storm day.

faq.q: Is gas still better than cordless?
faq.a: For deep or heavy snow, yes. For moderate snow, a premium cordless is quieter and easier. The right choice often comes down to your worst storm rather than your average one.
If you see more than a foot of snow or plow ridges, yes. A blown-in drift beside the garage counts as deep snow for this purpose.

faq.q: How long do the batteries last?
faq.a: Two 6Ah packs on the EGO 21-inch give the longest runtime in this list. Plan on swapping at the halfway point of a long driveway.

faq.q: Is an electric start worth it?
faq.a: In cold climates, yes. It needs an outlet near the machine. An extension cord rated for outdoor use is required for the PowerSmart's electric start, so test the start before the first storm.

faq.q: Can I use a single-stage on gravel?
faq.a: No. Use a two-stage with skid shoes. Skid shoes also protect pavers and decorative stone from the housing.
Drain or stabilize fuel; store batteries indoors. A tarp keeps dust and moisture off the engine while parked.
